content: Peripheral nerve blocks involve the administration of local anesthetics around a nerve to provide anesthesia or analgesia. However, their use for postoperative pain relief is limited by the relatively short duration of their analgesic effects, often necessitating alternative pain management strategies once the block wears off. To address this limitation, various adjuvants, including dexamethasone administered either perineurally or intravenously, have been investigated for their potential to extend the duration of analgesia. The primary objective of this study was to assess the efficacy and safety of perineural dexamethasone compared to placebo, intravenous dexamethasone compared to placebo, and perineural dexamethasone compared to intravenous dexamethasone when used as an adjunct to peripheral nerve blocks for postoperative pain management in surgical patients. A comprehensive search of multiple databases, including the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials, MEDLINE, Embase, and others, was conducted up to April 25, 2017. Additional sources such as trial registries, Google Scholar, and conference abstracts from major anesthesiology societies were also reviewed. Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) involving patients undergoing upper or lower limb surgeries and comparing the aforementioned interventions were included. The analysis included 35 RCTs with a total of 2,702 participants aged 15 to 78 years. Most studies (33) involved upper limb surgeries, while only two focused on lower limb surgeries. Thirteen studies were assessed as having a low risk of bias, while the remaining 22 had a high or unclear risk of bias. Perineural Dexamethasone vs. Placebo The duration of sensory block was significantly longer in the perineural dexamethasone group compared to placebo, with a mean difference (MD) of 6.70 hours (95% confidence interval [CI]: 5.54 to 7.85). Postoperative pain intensity at 12 and 24 hours was significantly lower in the perineural dexamethasone group compared to placebo, with MDs of -2.08 (95% CI: -2.63 to -1.53) and -1.63 (95% CI: -2.34 to -0.93), respectively. However, no significant difference was observed at 48 hours. Cumulative 24-hour postoperative opioid consumption was significantly reduced in the perineural dexamethasone group compared to placebo, with an MD of -19.25 mg (95% CI: -32.51 to -5.99). The quality of evidence was rated as very low for pain intensity at 12 hours and low for other outcomes. Intravenous Dexamethasone vs. Placebo The duration of sensory block was significantly longer in the intravenous dexamethasone group compared to placebo, with an MD of 6.21 hours (95% CI: 3.53 to 8.88). Postoperative pain intensity at 12 and 24 hours was significantly lower in the intravenous dexamethasone group compared to placebo, with MDs of -1.24 (95% CI: -2.44 to -0.04) and -1.26 (95% CI: -2.23 to -0.29), respectively. No significant difference was observed at 48 hours. Cumulative 24-hour postoperative opioid consumption was significantly reduced in the intravenous dexamethasone group compared to placebo, with an MD of -6.58 mg (95% CI: -10.56 to -2.60). The quality of evidence was moderate for the duration of sensory block and pain intensity at 24 hours, but low for other outcomes. Perineural Dexamethasone vs. Intravenous Dexamethasone The duration of sensory block was significantly longer in the perineural dexamethasone group compared to the intravenous group, with an MD of 3.14 hours (95% CI: 1.68 to 4.59). Postoperative pain intensity at 12 and 24 hours was lower in the perineural dexamethasone group compared to the intravenous group. However, the differences did not meet the predetermined threshold for clinical significance (MDs of -1.01 [95% CI: -1.51 to -0.50] and -0.77 [95% CI: -1.47 to -0.08], respectively). No significant difference was observed in pain intensity at 48 hours or in cumulative 24-hour postoperative opioid consumption. The quality of evidence was moderate for the duration of sensory block and pain intensity at 24 hours, but low for other outcomes. Adverse Events Five serious adverse events were reported across the included studies. One block-related event (pneumothorax) occurred in a trial comparing perineural dexamethasone and placebo, but the group allocation was not specified. Four non-block-related events were reported in trials comparing perineural dexamethasone, intravenous dexamethasone, and placebo. These included two hospitalizations in the placebo group (one for a fall and one for a bowel infection), one case of Complex Regional Pain Syndrome Type I in the placebo group, and one case of pneumonia in the intravenous dexamethasone group. The quality of evidence for adverse events was rated as very low due to the limited number of events. Authors' Conclusions Lowto moderate-quality evidence suggests that both perineural and intravenous dexamethasone, when used as adjuvants to peripheral nerve blocks in upper limb surgeries, can prolong the duration of sensory block and reduce postoperative pain intensity and opioid consumption. There is insufficient evidence to determine the efficacy of dexamethasone as an adjuvant for peripheral nerve blocks in lower limb surgeries, and no evidence is available for pediatric populations. The findings may not be generalizable to patients at risk of dexamethasone-related adverse events, as such individuals were likely excluded from the included trials. Ongoing trials registered on ClinicalTrials.gov may provide additional insights and potentially alter the conclusions of this review.
